• Origin: Asia
  • Growth rate: Medium
  • Height: 10-30+ cm (after two months in the tank)
  • Light demand: Low
  • CO2: Low

• Other names: Water trumpet, Wendt's water trumpet, Green Wendtii Catacomb, Brown Wendtii Crypt
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: low to medium
  • Optimal pH: 6.5 – 8.0
  • Optimal GH: 8 – 18
  • Optimal temperature: 24 – 28 °C
  • Substrate: needed
  • Growth rate: slow
  • Placement in tank: mid-ground
  • Average height: 15 – 20 cm
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: runners
  • Colour: red, green, bronze or even purple

Cryptocoryne wendtii is prized as a durable, low-maintenance and easy plant. It generally does not require strong lighting, fertilization or CO2 supplementation, which makes it a great choice even for beginners. A major problem, however, is the identification of its many varieties.

Due to the ever-increasing demand in the ornamental aquatic plant industry, Cryptocoryne wendtii has been overharvested in its natural habitat. As a result, it is declared a critically endangered species on the Red List of Sri Lanka (IUCN, 2012). At present, collection from wild habitats is forbidden. However, this prohibition does not apply to plants that are proven to have been grown and propagated in nurseries.

Cryptocoryne wendtii was originally described as coming from Thailand. Nowadays it is confirmed that this species is endemic to the northwestern part of Sri Lanka.

The aquarium trade has become a major pathway of biological invasions. As a result, Cryptocoryne wendtii has also become established in Florida in the United States.

Important: Non-native species (plants and animals) should never be released out of their natural range. They may carry unidentified organisms, become invasive and alter ecosystems, causing the loss of native species and major economic consequences. NEVER release non-native species into the wild!

Cryptocoryne wendtii is usually found as solitary colonies confined to the upper parts of slow-moving freshwater streams and shallow rivers.

This species can grow either fully submerged or on the banks around the edges of the water (the so-called littoral zone), where its shoots and leaves may develop above water level.

In nature, this plant also benefits the ecosystem by preventing soil erosion with the help of its rhizomes that grow deep into the substrate.

Small varieties (such as var. nana) can be grown even in nano tanks. In general, however, the species requires some space because of its growth potential, and it does not like to be densely planted. The recommended minimum tank size is about 40 litres, which gives the plant sufficient room, especially when horizontal shoots start to spread. This makes it an ideal mid-ground plant for most tank sizes.

Aquarium plant from tissue culture in closed cup. Depending on your aquarium setup wendtii 'Green' can reach a height of 10-30 cm with rosettes ranging from 8-15 cm wide. When grown in an open space the leaves will virtually lie on the bottom. Like most other Sri Lanka Cryptocorynes, it also grows well in hard water. Easy to grow, it thrives in almost all conditions, even in the shadow of larger plants.

Fertilization: although it has a large root system, the plant also feeds from the water column and responds quite favourably to fertilizers. If you do not have a nutrient-rich substrate, add root tabs, and dose liquid fertilizer in the water column from time to time. It benefits from macro- and micronutrients, which sustain healthy growth and best colouration. However, according to a study, an excessive amount of nutrients suppresses its growth.

If you keep shrimp with it: a high level of CO2 and copper (found in most fertilizers) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Care: it is easy to care for. It is quite slow-growing; under optimal conditions it rarely grows more than 2.5 cm in a couple of weeks, and generally takes a month to grow a few (2 – 4) shoots. Do not expect a beautiful aquascape any time soon, but you will not have to cut it back or replace it often. It is relatively sensitive to substrate vacuuming that disturbs the roots. There is no need to trim submersed leaves; if there is excessive growth or old leaves, remove them directly from the rootstock.

Planting

Avoid planting in one large clump; divide the bunch into smaller clumps and space them at least 7 – 10 cm apart, because they branch out in width and do not like heavy density – plants compete for nutrients, which affects their health.

An optional but highly recommended step is to cut off all the leaves before planting. Cryptocoryne is well known for 'crypt melt' after planting; this is how the plant adapts to a new environment, and professional aquascapers recommend cutting all leaves down right away so the plant saves energy for adapting and new growth. If the plant is tissue-cultured (in vitro), there is no need to cut off the leaves.

Take the plant out of the rooting medium and wash it carefully with a soft brush in tap water. Use tweezers to gently place it into the substrate, with the rhizome buried beneath the substrate. Then do not disturb the plant.

Propagation

Cryptocoryne wendtii does not produce seeds; it can propagate only vegetatively by rhizome. This type of propagation is slow, which makes the species susceptible to extermination in the wild.

The plant produces runners bearing independent daughter plants. Once a daughter plant has 3 – 5 leaves it starts developing its own roots and can be safely cut off from the mother rhizome. In the aquarium it can also be propagated by dividing large clusters into small ones.

Important: unlike other rhizome plants (such as Anubias or Java fern), Cryptocoryne wendtii cannot be attached to hard surfaces (rocks, driftwood, etc.). It will die.

Dry start method

Most Cryptocoryne species are amphibious and can be cultivated submersed or emersed. Experiments showed that Cryptocoryne wendtii had the best growth and survival when grown emersed, which also makes it a great choice for paludariums.

  • Instead of filling the tank with water after planting, add only enough water to reach the surface of the lowest part of the substrate.
  • Cultivate the plant in a nutrient-rich substrate.
  • Spray water regularly to provide high humidity (around 80%).
  • Cover the top of the tank with cling wrap to maintain humidity.
  • Fill the tank with water when the plant's growth kicks off.

Even though the plant may melt afterwards, it will grow back much stronger and faster because it will already have a well-developed root system.

Problems

  • Melting: 'Cryptocoryne disease' is probably the most common problem. It generally occurs when the plant is transferred from an emersed to a submersed environment, is moved, or when water parameters change suddenly and significantly. Crypts can also be quite sensitive to high nitrates. Solution: don't panic when the crypts melt; by doing so the plant conserves as much energy in its roots as possible. In most cases the leaves regrow within 2 – 3 weeks.
  • Relocation: relocating an old plant can be a real problem. It forms large, massive roots that can uproot a huge part of the tank. Solution: be careful and take it out very slowly.
  • Slow growth: plants show slow or stunted growth when there are insufficient trace elements in the substrate and water. Solution: remedy these inadequacies by adding root tabs and liquid fertilizers periodically. Always test the tank water and ensure it holds ample nutrients.

Cryptocoryne wendtii is hardy and can adapt to a variety of water conditions (even slightly brackish water). It grows under low to medium lighting, warm water, neutral pH and moderately hard water.

Temperature: the optimum is 24 – 28 °C, as the plant grows best in warm water. It can also easily tolerate lower temperatures (such as 20 – 22 °C), but will grow slower.

pH: prefers 6.5 – 8.0; a neutral pH is more suitable. Monitor pH regularly with an accurate test kit. Avoid large pH fluctuations, which can cause melting. The pH of the water affects the plant's nutrient uptake and is therefore a significant factor for growth.

Hardness: adaptable to a wide range of hardness, but grows best at 6 – 18 GH. It does not like water that is too soft, especially if the plant is moved from hard to very soft water.

Lighting: the plant needs moderate lighting to photosynthesize and grow optimally. Moderate light gives more compact, bushier growth with lots of runners and more pronounced colour. Under low light the colour will be slightly different and upward growth is triggered. Keep lighting on for up to 10 – 12 hours daily.

Substrate: it needs a nutrient-rich substrate. It is a heavy root feeder, although it can also take nutrients from the water column. When submerged it develops a very strong root system that can reach 30 cm or more, so provide a substrate at least 5 cm deep to allow easy spread and anchorage of the roots.

It can also be kept in sand or gravel, but you will have to regularly use root tabs and liquid fertilizers. According to a study, plants grown in river sand enriched with commercially available fertilizer had the highest dry weight gain and survival compared with plants grown in top soil and river sand mixed at 1:1, 1:2 and 1:3 ratios, because river sand lets the roots retain air. Ideally the substrate consists of coarse particles of about 2 – 5 mm, so the plants hold firmly and feed better.

Different substrates can be combined: for example porous stone, small gravel or coarse sand as the first layer (for better oxygenation) and a nutrient-rich substrate (such as ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Caribsea Eco-Complete, Seachem Flourite Black Sand) as the second layer.

Water flow: it does not like strong flow. In nature it is often found in slow-moving freshwater streams and rivers.

CO2: supplementation is optional. It can grow in low-tech tanks, but growth tends to be less bushy and very slow. As with most aquatic plants, adding CO2 improves growth rate and appearance.
Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Green' presents beautiful, green leaves. A fresh green group of Cryptocoryne wendtii 'Green' will decorate any tank.

Taxonomy

In 1828, Russian botanist Friedrich Ernst Ludwig von Fischer (1782 – 1854) described the genus Cryptocoryne for the first time. Since then, more than 60 species of Cryptocoryne have been described. In 1958, Dutch botanist Hendrik de Wit (1909 – 1999) described Cryptocoryne wendtii as a new species. In 1975, based on morphological comparisons, Czech botanist Karel Rataj (1925 – 2014) revised the genus and described four varieties: var. jahnelii, var. krauteri, var. nana and var. rubella. Since then at least 12 new varieties have become known in the aquarium hobby, but none of them is scientifically approved yet.

Etymology

The name Cryptocoryne has Greek roots: 'Krypto' meaning hidden and 'Coryne' meaning knobby bud or club-shaped, a reference to the flower. The species was named in honour of German botanist Albert Wendt (1887 – 1958), who had a special interest in the genus.

Description

Cryptocoryne wendtii is a perennial, rhizomatous aquatic plant. It has a wide range of leaf colour and shape variations, which gives it high market demand. According to some studies, in nature it is also considered an herbaceous perennial – a plant that dies down each year but whose roots remain alive and send up new growth each year.

  • Plant size: a medium-sized plant, growing up to 30 cm. In aquariums the average is usually 15 – 20 cm.
  • Growth form: can be grown emersed or submersed.
  • Leaf size: when submersed, the leaves are long and lanceolate, up to 25 cm long and 5 cm wide. In open aquariums, where it grows above the surface, the aerial leaves are oblong with a round or heart-shaped base, usually 8 to 10 cm long and 2 – 3 cm wide.
  • Colour: the leaves are usually brownish-green or olive green on the upper side and pale to reddish-green or purple on the underside. The reddish-brown colour is mainly due to anthocyanidin in the leaves.
  • Structure: the bold midrib has 3 – 4 pairs of lateral veins. The upper surface has short, brown or dark wavy markings or striations. The plant has thin rhizomes and runners.

It is a flowering plant. The flower grows from the centre of the plant and has a tubular appearance. Flowers (usually red and brown) form only above the surface.

Varieties

This species is the most diverse of any Cryptocoryne. The four main (semi-official) forms:

  • var. jahnelii (also called Cryptocoryne brown): the largest variation, up to 40 cm. Leaves are wide (up to 5 cm) and corrugated, usually brown to dark brown. Should be grown in a tall tank and placed in the middle, back or near the side walls.
  • var. krauteri: formerly also known as Cryptocoryne Augustifolia. Relatively small (up to 12 cm) and narrow (up to 2 cm) leaves, brown on the upper side and reddish on the underside, with wavy edges. Slow growing; better placed in the foreground.
  • var. nana: the smallest variety in the hobby, about 10 cm high. Leaves are dark brown with oblique, darker strokes on the upper side and reddish on the underside, with corrugated edges. It produces lots of runners close to the mother plant, so thin them out regularly. Place in the foreground in groups of several plants.
  • var. rubella: rather small (12 – 15 cm) with relatively wide leaves (up to 2.5 cm) with large corrugated edges. Very dark, probably the darkest variety, but silvery on the underside. Its rosette shape looks extremely decorative.

Other varieties:

  • var. wendtii: also known as Cryptocoryne lutea and Cryptocoryne Wendt broadleaf. Leaves 15 – 20 cm long and up to 5 cm wide, oblong with a round or heart-shaped base, pale green to brown on the upper side.
  • var. Tropica: named after the nursery Tropica. Grows 10 – 15 cm. Leaves are dark green to brown with a hammered pattern and grow almost prostrate.
  • var. Latifolia: grows 12 – 15 cm. Leaves are narrow, dark green to brown, with wavy edges and small corrugation on large bends.
  • var. Fasianus: up to 25 cm, rich emerald colour, leaves with brown longitudinal veins.
  • var. Flamingo: pinkish leaves. Rare and cultivated only in labs; much more sensitive than other Cryptocorynes.
  • var. Lutea: up to 30 cm, bright green with brown parts.
  • var. Mi Oya: found only in the Mi Oya river. Red-brown, slightly hammered leaves. Grows up to 30 cm.
  • Also: Green Gecko, Florida Sunset, Retrotutea, Bullosa, Indonesia.

In most cases it is extremely difficult (if possible at all) to tell these varieties apart. They may change significantly (size, colour and even shape) depending on tank conditions, and may look different in different areas of the same tank depending on temperature, water flow, lighting, etc. Cryptocoryne wendtii, Cryptocoryne beckettii, Cryptocoryne walkeri and Cryptocoryne undulata are also very closely related and look very similar. According to a study, they have a rather uniform spathe structure but differ slightly in colour:

  • C. beckettii: spathe with an olive-yellow limb and a reddish-purple or brown collar.
  • C. walkeri: bright green to yellow limb and a collar zone of the same colour as the limb.
  • C. wendtii: yellow to purplish-brown limb and brown to black-purple colour.
  • C. undulata: cream-yellowish to brownish limb with a collar of the same colour.

As a result, you cannot be sure which variety you have, and many of the fancy names may just be a marketing move.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: forms a lush bush that complements the aesthetics of the aquarium.
  • No overshadowing: it does not grow fast and will not choke other plants.
  • Prevents gas pockets: its well-developed root system helps break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate. Hydrogen sulfide pockets (H2S, smells like rotten eggs) can be dangerous to fish or shrimp.
  • Oxygenation: helps generate oxygen in the tank water.
  • Hiding place: serves as cover and shade for inverts and small fish.
  • Foraging place: acts as a buffet of biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.

Compatible tankmates

It can be paired with many aquatic species, though it is better suited to community tanks with small peaceful fish and inverts that won't rip the leaves apart.

  • Fish (for example bettas, swordtails, tetras, harlequin rasbora, danios, clown killifish, cherry barbs, panda garra, albino bristlenose pleco, platies, guppies, Endlers, mollies, otocinclus catfish, pygmy cory catfish).
  • Dwarf shrimp such as Neocaridina (Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Snowball, Black Rose, Orange Sakura, Green Jade, Rili) or Caridina (Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Tiger), Amano shrimp, ghost shrimp, bamboo shrimp, vampire shrimp. Basically any shrimp species can be kept with it.
  • Freshwater snails (Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails).

Avoid or be careful: never keep it with most crayfish or freshwater crabs, which will most likely tear up the foliage and uproot the plant. Also avoid aggressive fish known to devour plants, including Texas cichlids, Front cichlids, Jack Dempsey, Red Devil and Oscars.

In conclusion

Cryptocoryne wendtii is easy to grow, requiring nothing more than low to medium light and some nutrition in the substrate. It has numerous varieties and a wide range of foliage colours. It tolerates varying water temperature and hardness, thrives without CO2 injection and needs only minimal care.
